questionText: The trial attracted ____ of a kind the family had spent two decades trying to avoid.
explanation: Suffix '-ity' on the bare adjective, giving an uncountable noun meaning media attention. Spanish 'publicidad' means advertising first and foremost, so the L1 reading of this sentence would be that the family was pursued by advertisements.

questionText: The minister has never ____ acknowledged that the figures were revised after their release.
explanation: Adverbial '-ly' attaches directly to the adjective without the '-al' that most '-ic' adjectives require, making this one of the few irregulars of its class. The expected *publically is wrong, and Spanish 'públicamente' offers no warning.

questionText: The gallery did remarkably little to ____ the exhibition, relying instead on word of mouth.
explanation: Verbalising '-ise/-ize' converts the adjective into a transitive verb; both spellings are standard and either is credited. Spanish 'publicitar' and 'publicar' are distinct, and the second means 'to publish', which is the error the infinitive slot invites.

questionText: Each ____ of the grant must submit an annual report on the use of the funds.
explanation: Stem mutation 'receive' > 'recipi-' plus agentive '-ent', a form no rule predicts from the base. Spanish 'recipiente' is a false friend of the first order: it means a container, not a person, so the L1 reading makes the grant an object rather than an award.

questionText: The board proved wholly ____ to any proposal that involved further borrowing.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus the mutated stem 'recept-' plus '-ive'. The 'v' > 'pt' alternation is the difficulty, and Spanish 'poco receptivo' is a two-word paraphrase that gives no model for the single-word negation.

questionText: The study sets out to measure ____ to unfamiliar accents among first-year undergraduates.
explanation: The 'recept-' allomorph plus '-ive' plus '-ity', a triple modification. The competing 'reception' names an event or a desk, so only the '-ivity' abstract noun expresses the measurable openness the sentence requires.

questionText: For an avowedly ____ man, he spent a remarkable amount of time in cathedrals.
explanation: Negative 'in-' assimilated to 'ir-' before 'r', plus adjectival '-ous', with loss of the nominal '-ion'. Spanish 'irreligioso' matches, but learners more often reach for 'non-religious', which the concessive 'for an avowedly' makes stylistically flat.

questionText: The novel's ____ is stylistic rather than doctrinal: the cadences are those of the King James Bible.
explanation: Adjectival '-ous' plus '-ity', a double modification naming exaggerated or performative piety rather than faith itself. Spanish 'religiosidad' is more neutral, so the faintly critical colouring of the English noun is lost in transfer.

questionText: She kept the ledger ____ up to date, recording every transaction on the day it occurred.
explanation: Adjectival '-ous' plus adverbial '-ly', here in the wholly secular idiomatic sense of 'scrupulously, without fail'. Spanish 'religiosamente' has the same extended use, but learners hesitate to apply a sacred word to bookkeeping and substitute 'carefully'.

questionText: Students who fall below the threshold in the diagnostic test are offered ____ classes.
explanation: Adjectival '-ial' with 'y' > 'i', denoting teaching intended to correct a deficiency. Spanish 'remedial' is rare; 'de refuerzo' is the usual phrase, so the English adjective is under-produced despite the transparent root.

questionText: The damp had already done ____ damage to the frescoes on the north wall.
explanation: Negative 'in-' assimilated to 'ir-' before 'r', plus '-able' with 'y' > 'i'. Spanish 'irremediable' is a true friend, though English prefers it to 'irremedial' precisely because the '-able' branch carries the sense 'cannot be put right'.

questionText: ____ of the contaminated site is expected to take the better part of a decade.
explanation: Verbalising '-ate' plus nominalising '-ion', a double transformation with a specialised environmental sense. Spanish 'remediación' exists in technical registers only; the everyday 'remedio' pushes learners towards the bare noun, which cannot head this clause.

questionText: The district was rezoned as ____, and the old warehouses were converted into flats.
explanation: Stem plus '-ent' plus '-ial', a double modification with the final 'e' lost. Spanish 'residencial' is a true friend; the difficulty is that the family also yields 'residual' and 'residency', which look alike but share no sense.

questionText: A ____ bitterness survived long after the formal reconciliation had been announced.
explanation: Suffix '-ual' on the stem, meaning 'left over'. This is the trap of the family: 'residential' concerns housing and 'residual' concerns remainder, and Spanish keeps them equally distinct as 'residencial' and 'residual', yet the English pair is routinely swapped.

questionText: The composer took up a two-year ____ at the conservatoire in Lyon.
explanation: Suffix '-ency' naming a formal period of attachment to an institution, as against 'residence', which names a dwelling or the fact of living somewhere. Spanish 'residencia' covers both, so the countable-appointment sense must be learned separately.

questionText: An ____ leadership allowed the crisis to deepen unchecked for the better part of a year.
explanation: Negative 'in-' assimilated to 'ir-' before 'r', plus '-ute' with 'v' lost from the stem. Spanish 'irresoluto' is rare, and learners substitute 'indecisive'; note that 'unresolved' describes questions, never people.

questionText: The ____ of the dispute owed rather more to exhaustion than to any feat of diplomacy.
explanation: Nominalising '-ution' with loss of the stem's 'v'. Spanish 'resolución' is a true friend, but the English noun also means a formal motion and a screen property, so context alone fixes the reading here.

questionText: The question of attribution remains ____ after more than two centuries of argument.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus the past participle; unlike the adjective 'irresolute', this form keeps the 'v' of the stem. The verb 'remains' takes a participial complement, which is what excludes the noun 'resolution' from the slot.

questionText: The patient proved entirely ____ to the standard course of treatment.
explanation: Negative 'un-' plus the mutated stem 'respons-' plus '-ive'; the final 'd' becomes 's' before every suffix in this family. Spanish 'no responde' is verbal, so learners produce a clause where English requires a single adjective.

questionText: What the survey actually measures is the ____ of local authorities to complaints from tenants.
explanation: The 'respons-' allomorph plus '-ive' plus '-ness', a triple modification. The obvious rival 'responsibility' is a different word entirely, and Spanish 'responsabilidad' actively encourages that confusion.

questionText: Each ____ was asked to rank the twelve statements in order of personal importance.
explanation: Agentive '-ent' on the unmutated stem, naming a person who answers a survey. Spanish 'encuestado' shares no root, and the English word is easily confused with 'respondee', which does not exist.

questionText: His ____ treatment of the founding myths offended a good many of his readers.
explanation: Negative 'in-' assimilated to 'ir-' before 'r', plus '-ent' with the final 'e' lost. Spanish 'irreverente' is a true friend; the trap is orthographic, since the doubled 'r' of the prefix boundary is regularly reduced to one.

questionText: The manuscripts are handled with a ____ bordering on outright superstition.
explanation: Suffix '-ence' replacing the final 'e' of the verb. The article 'a' licenses this normally uncountable noun in the sense 'a particular kind of awe', and Spanish 'reverencia' also means a bow, a sense English does not carry here.

questionText: The biography adopts a ____ tone that blunts whatever critical edge it might have had.
explanation: Suffix '-ence' plus adjectival '-ial', a double modification. The shorter 'reverent' describes a person who feels awe, whereas '-ential' describes the manner or tone that expresses it, which is what modifies 'tone' here.

questionText: The instruction is grammatically well formed and yet entirely ____.
explanation: Negative prefix 'non-' plus the stem with the final 'e' lost plus '-ical', a double modification. Spanish 'sin sentido' is a phrase, so learners produce *senseless here; that word exists but implies pointless brutality rather than meaninglessness.

questionText: Resources were ____ squandered on a system that was obsolete before it was even installed.
explanation: Privative '-less' plus adverbial '-ly', a double modification meaning 'pointlessly'. The contrast with the previous item matters: '-less' gives futility, whereas 'non-' plus '-ical' gives incoherence.

questionText: Prolonged ____ deprivation produces hallucinations in the great majority of subjects.
explanation: Suffix '-ory' with loss of the final 'e', meaning 'relating to the senses'. The near neighbours 'sensitive', 'sensible' and 'sensual' are all wrong here, and Spanish 'sensible' means 'sensitive', which compounds the confusion.

questionText: In her account, style and argument are ____: neither can be assessed without the other.
explanation: Negative 'in-' plus '-able' with loss of the verbal '-ate'. Spanish 'inseparable' is a true friend, but the English base is spelled with 'par', not 'per', and *inseperable is among the most frequent errors in the whole family.

questionText: The ____ movement took nearly a third of the vote in the northern provinces.
explanation: Suffix '-ist' on the truncated stem, naming an adherent of political secession. Spanish 'separatista' matches; the trap is that learners often supply 'separatism', the doctrine, where the attributive slot before 'movement' needs the adherent form.

questionText: The ____ of powers is the constitutional principle genuinely at stake in this appeal.
explanation: Nominalising '-ion' replacing the verbal '-ate'. Spanish 'separación de poderes' is the exact equivalent, so the real risk is the 'a' of the second syllable, which the English spelling preserves and the pronunciation obscures.
